title: Frequencies of Shortest Supersequences
statement:
Each string in `words` is made of exactly two lowercase English letters. A string is a *common supersequence* of `words` when every word can be read inside it as a subsequence (the word's letters appear in it in the same order, not necessarily next to each other). Only common supersequences of the minimum possible length matter here.

Describe such a string by its letter counts: an array of 26 integers whose entry `0` is the number of `'a'`s, entry `1` the number of `'b'`s, and so on through `'z'`. Return the count arrays of all shortest common supersequences, listing each distinct array once (strings that are rearrangements of each other share one array). The arrays may come in any order.
constraints: Every word uses lowercase English letters, and all words together use at most 16 distinct letters
All strings in words are distinct
notes:
## Intuition

Trying strings of growing length until one contains every word works, but explodes fast. Two facts shrink the search. Every letter of the words appears at least once, and none ever needs more than two copies: a letter written at the very start and again at the very end comes before and after everything else, so it satisfies every word it is part of. A candidate is therefore fixed by choosing which letters appear **once**; the rest appear twice, and the length is `2k` minus the number of once letters, for `k` distinct letters.

The once letters must sit in one order where, for every word `xy` made of two once letters, `x` comes first; a word `xx` needs two copies of `x`. Read each word `xy` as an edge `x → y`: a set of once letters works exactly when the edges among its letters form no cycle (a self-loop counts). The shortest supersequences come from the largest such sets.

## Approach

1. Number the distinct letters `0..k-1` (`id` and `letters`).
2. For each word, set the first letter's bit in `before[second]`.
3. For each bitmask `once`, look for a letter `v` in it with no `before` bit inside `once`. If one exists, `once` is orderable exactly when `once` without `v` is; if none exists, every letter has a predecessor in the set, so it contains a cycle.
4. Track `size[once]` and the largest orderable size `most`.
5. For every orderable set of size `most`, output 1 for its letters, 2 for the other letters of the words and 0 elsewhere.

## Example 1, step by step

`a` gets index 0 and `b` index 1. Word `"ab"` puts `a` into `before[1]`; `"ba"` puts `b` into `before[0]`. The set `{a}` has no predecessor inside it, so it is orderable, and so is `{b}`. In `{a, b}` both letters have a predecessor, so it is not. `most = 1`, which gives `[1, 2, 0, …]` (from `"bab"`) and `[2, 1, 0, …]` (from `"aba"`).

## Complexity

- Time: O(m + 2^k · k) for `m` words: each of the `2^k` sets scans at most `k` letters, and `k <= 16`.
- Space: O(2^k) for `orderable` and `size`.

## Pitfalls

- A word like `"aa"` must make `a` its own predecessor; otherwise `a` could wrongly be written once.
- Only edges between two once letters matter; a doubled letter satisfies all its words on its own.
- Letters that appear in no word keep the count 0, not 1.
- Different strings with equal counts are one answer; each chosen set yields exactly one array.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `id`, `letters` | maps between a letter and its index among the `k` distinct letters |
| `before[v]` | bitmask of letters that some word puts before letter `v` |
| `once` | bitmask of the letters written once |
| `orderable[once]` | whether those letters can be ordered without breaking any word |
| `size[once]` | how many letters `once` holds |
| `most` | the largest orderable set size |
| `freq` | the 26 letter counts of one answer |
